title: Tandem and twin submerged-arc welding of high-strength, low-alloyed structural steels for tubular applications
abstract: Abstract Multi-wire submerged arc welding (SAW) techniques offer potential advantages for welding structural steels, but their effects on weld geometry, heat input, microstructure, and local hardness must be carefully evaluated. This study investigates the applicability of advanced submerged arc welding (SAW) techniques employing multiple wires configurations, namely tandem arc and twin arc with cold wire addition. The twin-ICE (Integrated Cold Electrode) technique, involving cold wire feeding, has recently gained attention for its potential to reduce the effective heat input and enhance the mechanical properties and structural integrity of welded joints. Nine specimens were fabricated: three using the tandem arc process and six using the twin-ICE configuration, varying the cold wire feeding ratio. The joints were evaluated through optical and scanning electron microscopy, stereoscopy, and microhardness mapping. Preliminary results indicate that cold wire addition may reduce the effective heat input, leading to a narrower HAZ, grain refinement, and a greater qualitative presence of acicular ferrite, consistent with the observed hardness response. While penetration depth may decrease with high cold wire ratios, optimized configurations achieve complete joint penetration (CJP) and improved bead geometry. The findings suggest that both SAW tandem and SAW twin-ICE processes are viable for welding HSLA steel plates up to 16 mm thick within industrially acceptable speed and energy ranges.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Piping systems are a vital component of infrastructure in numerous sectors. Welding is an essential process in the production and assembly of pipes, particularly those with large diameters. Currently, approximately two-thirds of pipes with seams worldwide are manufactured using welding [ 1 ]. Submerged arc welding (SAW) is one of the most widely used welding processes due to its high productivity, ease of mechanization, deep penetration, and high welding speeds [ 2 ]. In addition, it offers the flexibility to utilize a range of techniques, including the use of single or multiple wires, which significantly enhances the deposition rate [ 3 ,  4 ]. Among the techniques that utilize multiple wires are tandem arc and twin arc configurations [ 5 ]. The primary distinction between these SAW technologies lies in the power supply: tandem arc requires each electrode to be powered independently, whereas twin arc uses a single power source for both wires. Typical SAW variations include wire addition with or without independent power sources, arranged in tandem or twin configurations. The addition of a non-energized (cold) wire has been reported in the literature as a strategy to increase deposition capacity in multi-wire SAW systems [ 6 ,  7 ].

Advanced SAW process variants, such as tandem arc and ICE (Integrated Cold Electrode) technologies [ 8 ], have demonstrated significant potential to meet the growing demands of the industry. These variants have been reported to reduce welding heat input relative to the material thickness [ 9 ], thereby enabling improved process control and enhanced toughness, alongside high deposition rates and welding speeds [ 10 ,  11 ]. The tandem arc configuration uses multiple independently powered wires, offering key advantages such as significantly higher deposition rates and welding speeds of up to 2.5 m/min, depending on the number of wires [ 12 ,  13 ]. ICE technology incorporates a third, unenergized wire into the system. This technology can increase the deposition rate by up to 200% and reduces heat input by melting the cold wire with energy provided by the main electrodes. An additional benefit is the reduction in heat-affected zone (HAZ) size and the improvement of mechanical properties such as toughness [ 14 ].

ASTM A572 Gr. 50 is a high-strength, low-alloy (HSLA) structural steel designed for applications requiring a combination of high mechanical strength, good weldability, and an excellent strength-to-weight ratio. This steel has a minimum yield strength of 345 MPa and a tensile strength of 450 MPa, making it ideal for structural components such as bridges, power and communication towers, and platforms in the oil industry [ 15 ]. ASTM A572 Gr. 50 is a hypoeutectoid steel composed of ferrite and pearlite, with proportions dependent on prior heat treatment [ 16 ,  17 ]. During welding, heat input can result in HAZ regions with grain size variations and a tendency for coarse grain growth, potentially compromising the material’s strength and toughness [ 18 ,  19 ]. SAW processes with tandem arc or ICE configurations help minimize these effects by precisely controlling heat input. This promotes thinner, more uniform microstructures and increases the fraction of acicular ferrite in both the HAZ and weld metal, thereby improving ductility and impact resistance [ 20 ]. Furthermore, these configurations enhance process stability and enable the formation of weld beads with more uniform geometries, which is crucial in applications where repeatability and quality are essential [ 21 ].

Therefore, it is important to study submerged arc welding processes and their variants to understand their impact on pipe production. In the field of structural pipe fabrication, these technological advancements provide a promising solution to challenges related to material handling and adaptability to various dimensions and thicknesses, offering a competitive edge in the market. This study presents an experimental investigation into the feasibility of using tandem arc and twin arc variants with ICE technology for welding ASTM A572 Gr. 50 steel pipes. A systematic approach was adopted, involving microstructural characterization, hardness testing, and geometric analysis of the weld seams.

sections.heading: Experimental procedures
paragraphs: High-strength structural steel ASTM A572 Gr 50 was used as the base metal. The chemical composition of the ASTM A572 Gr. 50 base metal was experimentally determined by optical emission spectroscopy (OES), whereas the yield and tensile strength values were obtained from the material supplier certificate (Table  1 ). Because the intended application of the welded joints is structural tubular components rather than process or power piping, the welding procedure and joint evaluation were developed using AWS D1.1/D1.1M:2020 as the primary technical reference. This standard was adopted as a guideline for aspects such as joint configuration, welding conditions, preheat considerations, and weld profile evaluation for carbon and low-alloy structural steels. Double-square groove welds were produced on butt joints without root opening using 16 mm-thick coupons measuring 300 × 600 mm for SAW tandem and 200 × 800 mm for SAW twin arc welding. The welds were performed in a flat position (1G), with the plates fixed while the torches were moving. Table 1 Chemical composition and mechanical properties of the base metal (Cedisa 2019) Chemical composition (%) Mechanical properties Equivalent carbon (%) C Mn P S Si Sy (MPa) Su (MPa) Sy/Su 0.15 0.68 0.035 0.009 0.19 345 450 0.77 0.28

The welding consumables used were AWS 5.23: F8A2-EA2-A4 wire with a diameter of 2.5 mm for twin-arc welding and AWS 5.17: F6A4-EL12 wire with a diameter of 4 mm for tandem-arc welding. For all welding conditions, a basic agglomerated flux with a basicity index of 1.6 was used, according to the manufacturer’s certificate, with the trade name OK FLUX 10.71. Table  2  shows the chemical composition and typical mechanical properties of the consumables, according to the manufacturer’s quality certificate. Table 2 Chemical composition and mechanical properties of the welding consumables Process Welding consumables Chemical composition (%) Mechanical properties Mn Mo C Si Sy (MPa) Su (MPa) A (%) Twin  + cold wire A5.23: EA2-A4 1.1 0.5 0.1 0.1 500 580 24 Tandem A5.17: F6A4-EL12 0.5 - 0.09  < 0.1 360 465 30

The welds were made with a single pass on each side, aiming to achieve complete joint penetration (CJP). The parameters were defined based on bibliographic research and technical data from open literature. Two Aristo AC/DC 1000 inverter power sources were used for the construction of the tandem SAW coupons, one for each wire. The system included two torches and two flux delivery systems, both mounted on a welding column. The torch configuration is shown schematically in Fig.  1 . The first torch (lead) was mounted at a 0° inclination with DC polarity, and the second torch (trail) at a 15° inclination with AC polarity. The distance between wires was 25 mm, with a stick-out of 25 mm for the lead wire and 30 mm for the trail wire. Fig. 1 a ) Tandem SAW device and  b ) torch configuration

For the twin arc welding, a feeder-wire system with cold wire addition was used. This technology is called ICE by Esab. The system uses a third, electrically insulated wire running parallel to the two energized wires within the same contact device. The third wire is fed by a single welding source and is added at a percentage of the energized wires’ feed rate. Figure  2  shows the torch system. The setup is mounted on a welding stand, with an automatic welding head coupled to the three-wire feeder and flux. A 1000 A Aristo AC/DC inverter was used as the power source. DC + polarity was employed to promote greater penetration. Once defined, the welding parameters were entered into the PEK control center, which manages the welding variables and provides all information at the end of the process. Fig. 2 a ) Twin ICE® device,  b ) detail of filler system and  c ) schematic ICE® technology

Before welding, the plate surfaces were mechanically brushed to remove loose oxides and surface contaminants. To minimize moisture absorption, the remaining flux was stored at 180 °C before reuse, according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. No intentional preheating was applied, and the plates were welded at room temperature. This condition is consistent with the minimum preheat and interpass temperature requirements reported for 16 mm-thick ASTM A572 Gr. 50 plates, according to AWS D1.1/D1.1M:2020. Since welding was performed in two passes, one on each side of the joint, the plate was flipped after the first pass, and the root side was mechanically cleaned before depositing the second pass.

After welding, transverse cross-sections were extracted from each joint. Visual inspection, metallographic preparation, and macrographic analysis were carried out. Based on the results, welding speed values were adjusted for both tandem and twin arc processes. Microstructural analyses were performed using optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Specimens were prepared metallographically by cutting transversely and embedding in bakelite. They were ground with 100 to 1200 mesh water grit paper, followed by polishing with 3 µm and 1 µm diamond paste. Two chemical etchants were used to reveal the microstructure: 5% Nital (5 mL HNO₃ + 95 mL ethyl alcohol) to delineate grain boundaries and distinguish ferrite and pearlite, and LePera reagent (1 g sodium metabisulfite in 100 mL + 4 g picric acid in 100 mL ethyl alcohol) to highlight bainite and martensite.

Microhardness evaluation was performed by Vickers microhardness mapping using an Emcotest Durascan G5 tester with a load of 500 g, a dwell time of 15 s, and a spacing of 0.5 mm between adjacent indentations. Each hardness map was constructed from approximately 2,200 individual indentations distributed across the weld metal, heat-affected zone, and adjacent base metal regions. The hardness distributions presented in this work correspond to spatial hardness maps obtained from individual measurements. Therefore, no average hardness values or standard deviations were calculated for the hardness maps. Finally, grain size in the base metal and in the CGHAZ of the SAW-tandem and SAW-ICE welds was measured from representative optical micrographs using the linear intercept method, according to ASTM E112-12, with grain-boundary intercepts counted manually. The scale bar included in each micrograph was used as the length reference. For each condition, two test lines arranged in an X pattern were superimposed on the selected CGHAZ micrograph, and the grain-boundary intercepts along each line were counted. The mean grain size was calculated from the total test-line length and the number of intercepts. The reported values correspond to the mean grain size and standard deviation obtained from the intercept measurements performed for each condition.

sections.heading: Evaluation of geometry and dilution of welded joints
Tandem weld joints
paragraphs: Figure  4  shows the welded joints for the three parameters used. Figure  4 a presents partial joint penetration (PJP), while Fig.  4 b and c shows complete joint penetration (CJP). To achieve adequate bead, overlap and ensure CJP, a penetration depth greater than 8 mm is necessary in each pass. Fig. 4 Macrographs of tandem arc welds:  a ) T160,  b ) T140 and  c ) T120

The data for reinforcement height, penetration, and bead width are presented in Table  5 . The most notable characteristics of the fabricated samples are the minimal penetration and width observed in T160, while the maximum values are found in T120. The lowest reinforcement is observed in T160, while T140 and T120 exhibit the highest reinforcement. Table 5 Geometric characteristics of welding beads produced by SAW tandem Sample Side Penetration (mm) Width (mm) Reinforcement (mm) Dilution (%) T160 1 7.6 ± 0.2 15.5 ± 1.3 2.9 ± 0.2 71.09 ± 3.8 2 7.9 ± 0.3 19.3 ± 2.5 3.1 ± 0.3 68.52 ± 2.6 T140 1 8.4 ± 0.1 18.8 ± 1.4 3.8 ± 0.3 65.65 ± 3.3 2 8.0 ± 0.4 18.6 ± 2.4 3.5 ± 0.4 65.58 ± 4.2 T120 1 10.0 ± 0.3 20.8 ± 1.8 3.8 ± 0.2 68.05 ± 3.4 2 8.4 ± 0.2 22.4 ± 2.2 3.5 ± 0.2 63.86 ± 4.3

To facilitate interpretation, graphs are presented in Fig.  5  constructed from the values listed in Table  5 . The limited penetration observed in T160 condition (Fig.  5 a) is attributed to the high welding speed, which results in insufficient heat input due to reduced interaction time between the heat source and the base metal that is melted and incorporated into the weld pool [ 22 ]. Consistent with the trends reported by Kiran et al. [ 23 ], and Singh et al. [ 24 ] lower welding speeds increased penetration in T140 and T120 (Fig.  5 a). However, although T140 showed improved penetration relative to T160, the bead overlap remained insufficient to ensure reliable CJP in continuous industrial applications. Fig. 5 Geometric measurements and dilution of the deposited strands by SAW tandem.  a ) Penetration,  b ) width,  c ) reinforcement, and  d ) dilution

Bead width depends on the lateral fluidity and volume of molten metal, both of which increase with heat input [ 25 ] as reflected in Fig.  5 b. Consequently, the lower welding speed used in T120 promoted wider beads, whereas T160 produced narrower deposits due to the reduced interaction time between the arc and the base metal. Similar trends have been reported by Farhat [ 26 ]. The increase in bead width and reinforcement observed at lower welding speeds is attributed to the larger molten pool and greater deposition per unit length. Similar trends have been reported in previous SAW studies [ 26 ,  27 ].

According to AWS D1.1/D1.1M:2020, Clause 7.23.3 (Groove welds), together with the acceptance creiteria specified in Tables 7.8 and 7.9 of the same standard, the face reinforcement for the 16 mm-thick double-sided butt joints evaluated in this study shall not exceed 1/8 in. (3 mm) in height. Based on this criterion, sample T160 satisfies the reinforcement requirement. However, its lack of penetration indicates that this condition is not suitable for achieving complete joint penetration. Thus, a compromise between reinforcement height and penetration must be considered, together with filler material consumption and dilution.

The dilution values, shown in Table  5  and Fig.  5 d, reflect the influence of heat input, penetration, and reinforcement areas. As Fig.  5 c, shows, the reinforcement height remains unchanged between T140 and T120, implying that reinforcement area increases with bead width. The wetting angle remains similar, suggesting comparable molten metal flow. Greater reinforcement and bead width were observed as direct results of reduced welding speed and increased energy input, leading to larger cross-sectional weld areas, especially in samples welded at lower speeds. This behavior is often associated with larger HAZ and increased reinforcement, as noted by Moeinifar [ 28 ] and Sailender [ 29 ].

As illustrated in Fig.  5 d, changes in heat input did not cause substantial variations in dilution. The analysis of all three welding conditions shows an average dilution of 67.1% ± 1.78%. The stability of this value, despite heat input variations of 17% and 33%, is attributed to the proportional relationship between penetration and reinforcement area, which maintains consistent dilution values under different welding conditions. Barbosa et al. [ 30 ] reported an average dilution of 57% at higher heat inputs than those used in this study. Sharma et al. [ 31 ] also observed a slight decrease in dilution with increased heat input, but their results demonstrated stable values across different levels, which agrees with Shen et al. [ 32 ]. In general, reinforcement, penetration, and bead width increase with heat input, while dilution values remain nearly constant [ 33 ]. T160 provides suitable dilution and reinforcement height, while T120 ensures complete joint penetration. From a structural welding perspective, lack of penetration is considered a critical discontinuity because it may reduce the effective load-bearing area and act as a stress concentrator under service conditions. Among the evaluated conditions, only T120 achieved complete joint penetration without penetration defects. Although this condition produced the widest bead and highest filler metal consumption, dilution remained comparable to the other welding conditions. Therefore, T120 was considered the most suitable parameter set for obtaining complete penetration under the investigated conditions.

sections.heading: Twin-arc ICE
paragraphs: Figure  6  illustrates the effect of varying cold wire percentage and welding speed on weld geometry in the twin-arc ICE process. Fig. 6 Macrographs of twin-arc ICE welds:  a ) I0V60,  b ) I20V55,  c ) I70V55,  d ) I20V40,  e ) I70V40, and  f ) I0V40

Among the tested parameters, only samples I0V60 and I20V55 achieved complete joint penetration (CJP), as shown in Fig.  6 a and b. Although sample I70V40 (Fig.  6 e) exhibited CJP, the penetration was minimal and insufficient for industrial applications. In contrast, samples I0V40, I20V40, and I70V55 (Fig.  6 c, d and f) exhibited lack of penetration. The values for penetration, bead width, face reinforcement, and dilution obtained from the SAW twin-ICE process are summarized in Table  6 . Table 6 Geometric characteristics of welding beads produced by SAW twin-ICE Sample Side Penetration (mm) Width (mm) Reinforcement (mm) Dilution (%) I0V60 1 8.2 ± 0.2 19.9 ± 0.8 3.3 ± 0.4 64.0 ± 1.4 2 8.6 ± 0.2 21.5 ± 0.8 4.1 ± 0.4 61.3 ± 1.4 I20V55 1 9.1 ± 0.2 24.8 ± 0.4 2.3 ± 0.7 71.1 ± 4.3 2 8.8 ± 0.2 25.7 ± 0.4 3.7 ± 0.7 62.5 ± 4.3 I70V55 1 8.2 ± 0.6 21.0 ± 0.4 4.4 ± 0.1 58.4 ± 1.8 2 6.9 ± 0.6 27.1 ± 3.1 4.1 ± 0.1 54.8 ± 1.8 I20V40 1 7.4 ± 0.1 30.9 ± 1.09 3.7 ± 0.3 56.9 ± 0.7 2 7.6 ± 0.1 33.0 ± 1.09 4.3 ± 0.3 56.9 ± 0.7 I70V40 1 7.9 ± 0.3 26.9 ± 0.68 5.2 ± 0.3 53.5 ± 1.4 2 8.6 ± 0.3 28.3 ± 0.68 4.5 ± 0.3 56.2 ± 1.4 I0V40 1 7.0 ± 0.5 30.1 ± 0.53 4.1 ± 0.4 50.9 ± 3.4 2 8.0 ± 0.5 31.1 ± 0.53 3.3 ± 0.4 57.8 ± 3.4

The effect of cold wire percentage (CFR) on weld geometry and dilution is depicted in Fig.  7 , using the data from Table  6 . Only samples I0V60, I20V55, and I70V40 achieved combined penetration greater than 16 mm, indicating CJP. Fig. 7 Geometric measurements and dilution of the deposited welds by SAW twin-ICE:  a ) Penetration,  b ) width,  c ) reinforcement, and  d ) dilution

The effect of CFR on penetration quantity remains inconclusive. At 400 mm/min, increasing CFR enhances penetration; however, the opposite trend appears at 550 mm/min (Fig.  7 a). While lower welding speeds and higher heat input tend to increase penetration, as seen in I20V40 and I70V40, excessive cold wire may reduce available energy for base metal melting. For instance, I20V55 (20% CFR) shows greater penetration than I70V55 (70% CFR), even though both were welded at the same speed (550 mm/min). This suggests that excess cold wire can lower arc energy density, affecting joint penetration. Notably, the heat input was constant for welds at 400 mm/min (4.70 kJ/mm) and 550 mm/min (3.42 kJ/mm), with CFR as the only variable.

Deposit width and face reinforcement (Fig.  7 b and c) were influenced by both welding speed and CFR. Lower welding speeds promoted wider beads and greater reinforcement due to the longer arc dwell time and the increased volume of deposited metal per unit length, as observed for I20V40 and I0V40. Increasing the CFR generally increased bead width and reinforcement by introducing additional filler metal into the weld pool. However, exceptions were observed, such as I20V55, which exhibited relatively low reinforcement despite a 20% CFR, likely due to its greater penetration and the resulting redistribution of molten metal along the fusion line.

Although higher penetration and heat input are generally linked to increased dilution, CFR plays a complex role. For example, I20V55 exhibits high dilution (71.1%), whereas I70V55, which has a higher CFR, exhibits lower dilution (58.4%), which is higher than that reported by Barbosa et al. [ 30 ] and Castro [ 34 ]. Excess cold wire reduces arc energy density, thereby decreasing base-metal melting and, consequently, dilution. Increased bead width, when accompanied by high filler metal input, can also reduce dilution. For instance, I20V40, with widths of 30.9 mm and 33.0 mm, shows moderate dilution (~ 56.9%), indicating that a larger filler contribution reduces the relative proportion of melted base metal. In this case, the reduced heat available to melt the base metal is offset by increased face reinforcement and deposit width, resulting in reduced dilution.

CFR and welding speed must be analyzed together because both parameters influence weld geometry and dilution [ 35 ]. Under the investigated conditions, complete joint penetration was achieved for selected combinations of CFR and welding speed, while excessive cold-wire addition tended to reduce penetration. Therefore, twin-arc ICE welding appears most suitable for 16 mm-thick plates when CFR remains below 70% and welding speeds are maintained between 400 and 600 mm/min.

sections.heading: Base metal
paragraphs: The base metal, ASTM A572 Gr. 50, exhibited a banded microstructure composed of pearlite and fine equiaxed ferrite, with an average ferrite grain size of 6.69 ± 0.50 µm, as shown in Fig.  8 . The banded structure improves the mechanical properties of the material, particularly fracture toughness [ 36 ]. The volume fractions of the ferrite (F) and pearlite (P) phases are 70.1% and 29.1%, respectively. The average hardness of the material is 132.0 ± 4.5 HV. Fig. 8 Microstructure of the base metal ASTMA A572 Gr 50. Ferrite (F) and pearlite (P)

sections.heading: Microstructure in SAW tandem welds joints
paragraphs: The cross-sectional morphology obtained for both welding processes showed a fusion zone (FZ) and a heat-affected zone (HAZ), which can be divided into coarse-grained HAZ (CGHAZ) and fine-grained HAZ (FGHAZ).

Regarding the tandem arc welds, the main microstructure components observed were grain boundary primary ferrite (PF(GB)), idiomorphic ferrite (PF(I)), Widmanstätten ferrite with aligned microphase (WF-FS(A)), Widmanstätten acicular ferrite (WF-AF) and bainite (B), as shown in Fig.  9 . These microstructures were observed in all CGHAZ; their apparent relative distribution within the HAZ morphology varied among the three weld beads. This variation suggests that the different thermal conditions during the welding process affected the formation and relative distribution of these microstructures in the HAZ. Fig. 9 Micrograph analysis of the tandem-arc weld cross section with OM and detail views with SEM, specimen T120.  a ),  b ) HAZ of the first weld bead,  c ) macrograph of the cross section,  d ),  e ) HAZ of the second weld bead,  f ),  g ) FZ of the first weld bead,  h ),  i ) FZ of the second weld bead

The morphology of WF-FS(A), which is derived from grain boundary ferrites, was observed to change with welding speed [ 37 ]. It was observed that the ferrite lamellae became thicker as the heat input increased. Another relevant change in the HAZ microstructure was the variation in average grain size. As shown in Table  7 , the highest heat input condition, T120, exhibited the largest average grain size, whereas T140 and T160 showed reductions of 35.2% and 31.1%, respectively, relative to T120. Although T160 had slightly higher grain size than T140, with an apparent increase of 6.3%, this difference is small and can be associated with the difficulty of accurately identifying grain boundaries in regions containing mixed ferritic, bainitic, and Widmanstätten morphologies. Therefore, T140 and T160 can be considered to exhibit comparable grain refinement within the limitations of the manual intercept method. Table 7 Average grain size for the SAW-tandem cross-sections Sample Grain size (µm) HI (kJ/mm) T120 117.6 ± 27.7 2.8 T140 76.2 ± 3.2 2.4 T160 81.0 ± 6.8 2.1

To verify the presence of martensite in the HAZ of T160, a chemical etching was performed using Le Pera reagent (Fig.  10 ). Furthermore, the presence of martensite-austenite (M/A) constituent has been identified in previous studies with comparable heat input, welding process and base metal [ 28 ]. This analysis focused on the T160 condition because it has the highest cooling rates, making it the most likely to contain martensite or tempered martensite. These microconstituents have been identified in similar processes reported in the literature [ 38 ,  39 ]. High cooling rates can bring the material to temperatures below those at which martensite forms before the WF-AF and bainite transformations can be completed. Fig. 10 a ) HAZ and FZ interface and  b ) CGHAZ etched with Le Pera, sample T160

The microstructural analysis did not reveal the presence of martensitic microconstituents. The blue portions occupy more space as they move away from the center of the bead, as shown in Fig.  10 . This can be explained by the fact that the cooling rates decrease with the distance from the center, which favors the formation of ferritic morphologies instead of bainitic ones.

The bainite identified in the optical microscopy analysis was distributed throughout the CGHAZ in the form of islands contained within the grains. SEM analysis allowed for a more detailed visualization of the bainite morphology (Fig.  11 ). A high degree of microstructural refinement was observed, consisting of bundles of elongated carbides of nanometric dimensions, highly dispersed in the ferritic matrix [ 37 ,  40 ]. Fig. 11 Detailed view of the bainitic microstructure observed at the HAZ of sample T160

Regarding FZ microstructures, PF(GB), PF(I), WF-FS(A) and WF-AF were observed, as shown in Fig.  9 , g, h. In addition, the microstructure exhibited a columnar growth profile characteristic of fusion zones in carbon steels and high-strength, low-alloy steels [ 41 ,  42 ].

The bainite (B) and Widmanstätten acicular ferrite (WF-AF) are formed by similar transformation mechanisms and differ mainly in their nucleation sites. WF-AF nucleates in inclusions present within austenitic grains, whereas bainite nucleates at boundaries between austenitic grains or between ferritic and austenitic grains. WF-AF nucleation also depends on the crystallographic compatibility with the inclusions present [ 43 ,  44 ]. WF-AF growth is a transformation by crystalline distortion accompanied by plastic deformation and leads to a high density of dislocations in the microstructure, which contributes to its mechanical strength [ 39 ].

If boundaries are present during solidification, bainite is kinetically favored over acicular ferrite (WF-AF). However, once allotriomorphic ferrite has formed along the grain boundaries, the formation kinetics of acicular ferrite are favored [ 45 ]. The predominant presence of WF-AF in the grain interiors and the extensive presence of primary grain boundary ferrite (PF(GB)) along the fusion zone suggest that a PF(GB) layer was formed along the grain boundaries during cooling, prior to reaching the nucleation temperature of bainite (B) or Widmanstätten acicular ferrite (WF-AF). Thus, the formation of WF-AF in the intragranular inclusions took precedence over the nucleation of bainite. The formation of inclusions due to the dissolution of lighter elements at the higher temperatures of the welding process is another factor favoring the transformation to acicular ferrite as discussed by Babu [ 45 ].

At T120, after PF(GB) had occupied the boundaries, the slower cooling rates allowed the nucleation and growth of WF-FS(A), shown in Fig.  9 g, from PF(GB). In contrast, at T140 and T160, this structure had less time to develop because the temperature at which WF-AF formation predominates was reached more quickly. Morphologically, WF-AF has a greater length-to-width ratio in one direction, giving it a needle-like shape when observed in two dimensions. Its morphological units arise with random orientation, forming chaotically intertwined sets. This characteristic morphology results from repeated shear transformations in the crystalline structure of the initial phase, leading to rapid diffusional growth of previously nucleated WF-AF microconstituents. This kinetic mechanism is analogous to that observed in bainite but differs in that it exhibits multiple directions of random radial growth [ 40 ].

Microstructural observations suggest a greater relative presence of WF-AF at higher welding speeds. This behavior is attributed to the higher cooling rates associated with lower heat input, which favor acicular transformations and limit grain growth. Conversely, lower welding speeds result in coarser microstructures and an increased apparent grain boundary ferrite content due to longer thermal exposure and lower cooling rates [ 46 ,  47 – 48 ].

Samples T160 and T120 with the lowest and highest heat input respectively were used for the microhardness maps of the tandem arc welds as shown in Fig.  12 . Increasing the heat input has been observed to reduce the hardness. This behavior is suggested by the microstructural components present and is the result of the thermal cycles imposed by the variation of heat input to the bead. T160 specimen shows hardness values between 170 and 200 HV in the weld bead. In the HAZ the values are between 150 and 170 HV. Meanwhile, the T120 specimen with greater heat input has lower hardness values in the HAZ, between 150 - 170 HV. The HAZ for the same specimen also occupied this range of values. The hardness values shown for specimen T160 are mainly due to the presence of acicular ferrite, which imparts greater hardness to the weld metal. In contrast, for sample T120, the hardness is reduced due to the grain coarsening in this weld bead [ 49 ]. Fig. 12 Microhardness maps of samples T160 and T120 tandem-arc welds

sections.heading: Microstructure in SAW twin-ICE welds joints
paragraphs: Figure  13  shows the microstructural analysis for the I20V55 sample using OM and SEM in the FZ and HAZ. In general, the same microstructural components with changes in morphology were observed for all parameters tested. The main microstructural components observed were, grain boundary primary ferrite (PF(GB)), idiomorphic ferrite (PF(I)), Widmanstätten ferrite with aligned microphase (WF-FS(A)), Widmanstätten ferrite with non-aligned microphase (WF-FS(NA)), Widmanstätten acicular ferrite (WF-AF) and bainite (B). However, increasing the heat input resulted in larger grains and a thicker existing microstructure. Previous studies have reported that adding a cold wire can reduce the heat available to the base material, thereby promoting grain refinement and altering the HAZ microstructure, while maintaining high deposition rates [ 6 ,  30 ,  50 ]. Fig. 13 Micrograph analysis of the twin-arc weld cross section with OM and detail views with SEM, specimen I20V55.  a ),  b ) HAZ of the first weld bead,  c ) macrograph of the cross section,  d ),  e ) HAZ of the second weld bead,  f ),  g ) FZ of the first weld bead,  h ),  i ) FZ of the second weld bead

The average grain size measured in the CGHAZ of the SAW-ICE samples are presented in Table  8 . Although the nominal heat input was calculated only from voltage, current, and welding speed, and therefore remained constant for samples welded under the same electrical parameters and travel speed, the cold wire ratio clearly affected the resulting grain size. For the conditions welded at 550 mm/min and 3.42 kJ/mm, increasing the CFR from 20 to 70% reduced the average grain size from 105.9 ± 11.5 µm to 80.8 ± 6.7 µm. Similarly, for the conditions welded at 400 mm/min and 4.70 kJ/mm, increasing the CFR from 0 to 20% and 70% reduced the average grain size from 199.6 ± 40.3 µm to 125.5 ± 16.1 µm and 105.9 ± 11.5 µm, respectively. This behavior supports the interpretation that part of the arc energy is consumed to melt the additional cold wire, thereby reducing the effective heat input available to heat the HAZ. As described by Kesavan et al. [ 51 ], and Rigdal [ 52 ], this reduction in effective heat input can promote a narrower and more refined HAZ, even when the nominal heat input remains unchanged. Regarding the FZ, the main microstructures observed were grain boundary primary ferrite (PF(GB)), idiomorphic ferrite (PF(I)), and Widmanstätten acicular ferrite (WF-AF). WF-AF was the predominant constituent. Increasing heat input promoted grain coarsening and thicker ferritic morphologies due to lower cooling rates, consistent with the observations of Thewlis [ 48 ] and David et al. [ 53 ]. Microstructural observations also indicated a reduced relative presence of WF-AF at higher heat inputs, in line with the findings of Barbosa et al. [ 30 ]. However, the evolution of fusion-zone microstructures is influenced by several interacting factors, including solidification conditions, prior austenite grain size, inclusion characteristics, distribution of alloying elements, dilution, and welding thermal cycles [ 50 ,  54 ]. Consequently, the effect of a single parameter cannot be evaluated independently. Although cold-wire addition reduces the effective heat input [ 53 ], no significant qualitative changes in the fusion-zone microstructure were observed across the investigated conditions. Instead, the most pronounced effects of cold-wire addition were observed in the heat-affected zone (HAZ), where grain refinement was evident.

The microhardness maps for the twin-arc beads with two different heat inputs are shown in Fig.  14 . Figure  14 a shows the map for the sample with 20% cold wire and a welding speed of 550 mm/min and Fig.  14 b represents the sample with 70% cold wire and the same welding speed of 550 mm/min. Increasing the cold wire content from 20 to 70% in the samples reduced the effective heat input and increased the hardness in the melt zone. This behavior can be explained by the microstructural changes, such as an increased in the presence of acicular ferrite and a reduced amount of grain boundary ferrite. In the HAZ region, sample I70V55 exhibits higher hardness values than sample I20V55. This difference can be attributed to the shorter exposure time to high temperatures, which results in grain refinement. [ 55 ,  56 ]. Fig. 14 Microhardness maps for 120V55 and 170V55 twin-arc welds

A similar increase in hardness associated with reduced effective heat input during cold wire addition was reported by Mohammadijoo et al. [ 6 ] for tandem arc weld. Ramakrishnan [ 50 ] describes the increase in hardness due to grain refinement, and points to acicular ferrite as the main factor responsible for the increase in this property in the melt zone. Finally, the increase in the proportion of cold wire in the molten pool may have influenced the increase in hardness in the weld metal due to the presence of molybdenum in the wire. According to Bhole et al. [ 57 ] and Sirin et al. [ 58 ], Mo additions of up to 0.4 wt% can be used to increase the proportion of acicular ferrite, which promotes an increase in hardness.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Both the SAW tandem and the SAW twin-ICE processes were successfully used to weld ASTM A572 Gr. 50 joints up to 16 mm thick. The results showed that the weld geometry, the characteristics of the heat-affected zone (HAZ), and the microstructural features were strongly influenced by welding speed, heat input, and the addition of cold wire. SAW tandem provided stable penetration and bead geometry, whereas SAW twin-ICE offered greater flexibility in controlling effective heat input and promoting HAZ grain refinement.

In the SAW tandem process, penetration and bead width increased with decreasing welding speed, due to a longer interaction time between the arc and the base material. Despite these geometric changes, dilution remained relatively constant at approximately 67%, indicating a proportional balance between penetration and reinforcement areas. Reinforcement height remained similar for the lower-speed conditions (T140 and T120), reaching values up to 3.8 mm.

For SAW twin-ICE welds, penetration was significantly influenced by the heat input (HI) and cold wire ratio (CFR). Only the I0V60, I20V55, and I70V40 configurations achieved complete joint penetration (CJP), with combined penetrations above 16 mm. Conversely, samples with high CFR, such as I70V55, exhibited reduced penetration due to heat redistribution to melt the cold wire. Bead width was greater in the low welding speed configurations, such as I20V40 (30.9–33.0 mm), owing to longer arc dwell time. Reinforcement height was positively correlated with CFR, reaching maximum values of 5.2 mm in I70V40, albeit with a decrease in dilution (53.5%) due to reduced base metal contribution to the weld pool.

The SAW tandem welded joints exhibited a heat affected zone (HAZ) divided into coarse-grained (CGHAZ) and fine-grained (FGHAZ) regions, with acicular ferrite (WF-AF), Widmanstätten-aligned ferrite (WF-FS(A)), and bainite (B) as the main microstructures observed. In the fusion zone (FZ), PF(GB), PF(I), WF-FS(A) and WF-AF were observed. Samples with lower welding speeds, such as T120, displayed a greater qualitative presence of idiomorphic ferrite (PF(I)) and grain boundary ferrite (PF(GB)), resulting from reduced cooling rates. In contrast, T160, with higher welding speed and lower heat input, exhibited a higher presence of acicular ferrite and more refined structures, which was consistent with the higher local HAZ hardness values ranging from 170 to 200 HV.

SAW twin-ICE welds showed that increasing the CFR may reduce the effective heat input available to the HAZ, which was associated with a tendency toward grain refinement and increased hardness in this region. In configurations such as I70V55, higher hardness was associated with the presence of acicular ferrite, driven by shorter exposure times to high temperatures. In the fusion zone, the main microstructures included acicular ferrite (WF-AF) and grain boundary ferrite (PF(GB)). Although CFR did not produce evident qualitative changes in the microconstituents observed in the fusion zone, the addition of cold wire improved thermal distribution and promoted grain refinement in the HAZ. The use of a moderate CFR (20%) provided a favorable balance between penetration, weld geometry, microstructural refinement, and microhardness response.

The formation and distribution of acicular ferrite (WF-AF) were relevant microstructural features influencing the local microhardness response of both welding processes. Controlling welding speed, heat input, and cold-wire addition proved effective for tailoring weld geometry, HAZ refinement, and local microhardness response in ASTM A572 Gr. 50 steel without compromising penetration or dilution.
